title: Two Hours and Two Minutes
subtitle: In November 1863 the star speaker talked for two hours and the president for two minutes. Only one of them had decided where he would land.

card.essence: A famous orator, a famous 272 words, and a note written the next morning. Why the speakers who sound most senior know their last sentence before they say their first.

intention: you'll see why strong speakers plan from the last sentence backwards, build a three-part landing plan, and use it to give a clear answer in under thirty seconds.
warmup: Think of someone who always gets to the point. What do they actually do differently from everyone else?
When someone gives a long answer, how long do you wait before you stop listening — and what do you do instead?
Before an important conversation, do you plan the first sentence, the last sentence, or neither?

vocab.heading: A · What do they mean here? Work it out from the context
vocab.intro: Read the sentence, guess the meaning of the word in bold, then reveal.

items.sent: Crowds waited quietly while the famous speaker delivered a two-hour oration from memory.
items.meaning: oration — a formal, public speech, usually long and carefully prepared.

items.sent: If you ramble, your listeners stop asking what you mean and start wondering when you will finish.
items.meaning: ramble — to talk for a long time in a confused or unfocused way, without a clear point.

items.sent: Her report was concise: three pages, one recommendation, nothing wasted.
items.meaning: concise — giving all the necessary information in very few words.

items.sent: Even his critics admitted that the speech was eloquent, though they disliked what it said.
items.meaning: eloquent — able to express ideas in a fluent, clear and persuasive way. The noun is eloquence.

vocab.heading: B · Which expression fits?
vocab.intro: Say the expression you would use, then reveal.

items.sent: You want the one thing that matters most after all the details have been taken away.
items.meaning: the bottom line — the most important fact or conclusion in a situation.

items.sent: The meeting is already late, so you stop the small talk and start on the real issue.
items.meaning: cut to the chase — to stop wasting time and deal directly with the most important thing.

items.sent: She began a confident sentence, then her voice became quieter and she never really finished it.
items.meaning: trail off — to become gradually quieter and stop speaking without completing what you were saying.

vocab.heading: C · Which word completes all three phrases?
vocab.intro: One missing word fits every phrase in the group. Say it, then reveal.

items.sent: ___ a speech  ·  ___ a verdict  ·  ___ bad news
items.meaning: deliver — to give a speech, a decision or a message formally; also to bring something to its destination.

items.sent: ___ a message  ·  ___ a feeling  ·  difficult to ___ in words
items.meaning: convey — to communicate an idea, feeling or piece of information so that it is understood.

items.sent: a few opening ___  ·  closing ___  ·  to make some brief ___
items.meaning: remarks — spoken comments, often short and formal, made on an occasion. A speaker "makes remarks"; a critic "remarks on" something.

vocab_use: Tell me about a speech or presentation you remember. Was it concise, or did the speaker ramble? What do you remember afterwards?
What is the bottom line of the last thing you read or watched? Say it in one sentence.
Who is the most eloquent person you know, and how do they deliver a difficult message?

story.heading: Part 1 — A field full of graves
paras: In the first days of July 1863, two armies fought for three days around a small Pennsylvania town called Gettysburg. By the end, the number of dead, wounded and missing was in the tens of thousands. Many of the Union dead were buried quickly, in shallow graves, in the fields where they had fallen.

The state decided to create a proper cemetery and to hold a ceremony to dedicate it. The organisers wanted the finest speaker in America to give the main address: Edward Everett, a former senator, Secretary of State and president of Harvard, known for speaking for hours without notes. He said he needed time to prepare, so the date was moved to 19 November.

Only then, in early November, did the organisers think to invite the president. Abraham Lincoln was asked to follow the main speaker with "a few appropriate remarks". It was an afterthought, and it sounded like one.
checks: Who was chosen as the main speaker, and what was he known for?
Why was the date of the ceremony moved?
What was Lincoln asked to do — and when?
answers: Edward Everett — a former senator, Secretary of State and president of Harvard, famous for long speeches given from memory.
Everett said he needed more time to prepare.
To make "a few appropriate remarks" after the main speaker; the invitation came in early November, only a couple of weeks before the ceremony.
story.discuss: Everett was given extra time and Lincoln was given a few weeks and a few minutes. Who had the harder task — the person who must fill two hours, or the person who must say something that matters in two minutes?

story.heading: Part 2 — Two hours, then two minutes
paras: On 19 November, Everett stood up and spoke for about two hours. His speech ran to roughly thirteen thousand words. It described the battle day by day, compared the dead to the heroes of ancient Greece and explained the causes of the war. Many people who were there considered it a magnificent performance.

Then Lincoln rose. His text had about 272 words and took around two minutes to deliver. It did not describe the battle at all. It said that the nation had been "conceived in liberty" and "dedicated to the proposition that all men are created equal", that the living must finish the work the dead had begun, and that government "of the people, by the people, for the people" should not disappear from the earth.

Lincoln had worked on those words for days beforehand, and there are several handwritten copies in which he changed small details. Reactions at the time were mixed: some newspapers praised the remarks, while others, divided by politics, hardly mentioned them or dismissed them.
checks: Roughly how long, and how many words, was Everett's speech?
What did Lincoln's speech leave out — and what did it say instead?
What is the evidence that Lincoln prepared carefully?
answers: About two hours and roughly thirteen thousand words.
It left out the details of the battle. Instead it said what the nation stood for and what the living now had to do.
He worked on the text for days, and several handwritten copies survive in which he changed small details.
story.discuss: Lincoln did not describe the battle. What does a speaker gain by leaving out most of what they know — and what is the risk?

story.heading: Part 3 — The note
paras: The next morning, 20 November, Everett wrote to Lincoln. He congratulated him and added one sentence that has been quoted ever since: he would be glad if he could flatter himself that he had come as near to the central idea of the occasion in two hours as Lincoln had in two minutes.

Lincoln replied the same day. He said that neither of them could have been excused from his part, Everett from making a long address or himself from making a short one, and that he was pleased to learn the little he had said was not entirely a failure.

Was Everett simply wrong to speak for two hours? Not necessarily. The crowd had come expecting a long oration, and the full story of the battle was worth telling. But the man who gave the longer speech was the one who admitted which of the two had reached the point. Today your listeners rarely have two hours. The question is whether you know your central idea — and whether you say it first.
checks: When did Everett write to Lincoln, and what did he say?
Why is it unfair to say that Everett was simply wrong?
answers: The next day, 20 November. He said he would be glad to have come as near to the central idea in two hours as Lincoln had in two minutes.
He said that neither man could have been excused from his own part, and that he was pleased the little he said was not entirely a failure.
The crowd expected a long oration and the full account of the battle had value. The occasion allowed for it — most of our conversations do not.
story.discuss: Everett said himself that Lincoln had reached the central idea faster. When has someone's short answer taught you more than a long one?

tool_tab.lead: The oldest advice about speaking is to know your ending before you begin. Stephen Covey made it the second of his seven habits in 1989: begin with the end in mind. Barbara Minto, who worked at McKinsey, taught consultants to open with the answer and then support it — her Pyramid Principle. The tool below turns that idea into three moves you can make in one breath: a point, one reason, and a stop.
how: Decide your landing first. Ask: what do I want them to know, decide or do when I finish? Write it as one sentence.
Say it first. Open with the answer itself: The short answer is…, My recommendation is…, What I need from you is…
Add one reason — the strongest, not all of them. The rest of the detail waits until someone asks for it.
Stop. End on your last word and let the silence do its work. If more is wanted, they will ask: Happy to go into detail.

sort.intro: These are sentences from rambling answers. What job does each one do in a landing plan? Choose, then check.

items.text: Well, I've been looking at this for quite a while now, and there's honestly a lot to say about it.
items.why: it announces that you will speak but says nothing; delete it.

items.text: We should move the launch to March.
items.why: it is the answer itself, in the first sentence.

items.text: The supplier cannot deliver the components before the end of February.
items.why: one concrete reason that supports the point.

items.text: It reminds me of something that happened on a completely different project last year.
items.why: it is a detour; keep it for later if anyone asks.

items.text: So that's my recommendation — I'd like a decision by Friday.
items.why: it closes the answer and says exactly what you need next.

items.text: Yes, we can finish by Friday.
items.why: a direct answer to a direct question.

items.text: Two of the three tests have already passed.
items.why: a fact that supports the point, short enough to say in one breath.

breaks: Delicate news. A blunt opening can sound cold. Keep the order but soften the delivery: I'm afraid the short answer is no.
You don't have a view yet. A forced point is worse than an honest one. Land on that instead: I don't have an answer yet. What I can tell you is…
Occasions and stories. Everett's audience had come for a long oration, and some stories need their journey. The plan is for answers, not for ceremonies.
discuss: Which would you find harder: saying the point first, or stopping after one reason? Why?
When is it wiser to give the background before the point?

grammar.name: Opening with the verdict
grammar.lead: Point-first speaking depends on a small set of openers that commit you to an answer in the first few words. Learn them as chunks: they are what you reach for when your mind is still planning the rest.
notes: Direct openers: The short answer is… · The bottom line is… · The upshot is… — followed by the answer. The short answer is no. The bottom line is that we cannot deliver by Friday.
Wh-cleft (focus on what matters): What I need from you is a decision. What worries me is the timeline. The first part names the topic; the verb is then delivers the point.

Recommendations: I recommend that + subject + base verb — I recommend that we postpone the launch. After recommend, suggest, insist and propose, the verb stays in the base form, even with he, she or it: I suggest that she attend, not attends.

exercises.heading: Base form after recommend
exercises.intro: Write the verb in brackets in the correct form.
items: 1. I recommend that the committee ___ (postpone) the decision until the figures arrive.
2. She insisted that every new employee ___ (be) given a written plan.
3. We suggest that he ___ (send) the revised budget before Thursday.
4. I'd propose that the two teams ___ (meet) once a week from now on.

exercises.heading: Choose the opener
exercises.intro: Use each word from the box once: recommend · upshot · short · bottom · need.
items: 1. The ___ answer is no — the building will not be ready in time.
2. What I ___ from you is a clear decision by the end of the day.
3. The ___ line is that we are spending more than we earn.
4. I ___ that we start again with a smaller team.
5. The ___ of all this is that the project will cost twice as much.

grammar.closing: Now say one answer to a question you were asked this week — using one opener from this page as your first words.

speak.intro: Plan the landing, then speak. Choose a task, start the timer, and talk.
speak.useful: “The short answer is…” · “My recommendation is that we…” · “The main reason is…” · “What I need from you is…” · “That's my view.”

tasks.label: Task 1 — Thirty seconds
paras: Pick one question: Should people finish what they start, even when it is no longer worth it? Is a meeting ever better than an email? Which matters more in a leader — being decisive or being right? Plan for ten seconds: your point, one reason, how you will stop. Then answer in thirty.

tasks.label: Task 2 — Say it again, shorter
paras: Think of a time you gave a long, unfocused answer. Tell me the question and then give the answer you wish you had given: point, one reason, stop.

tasks.label: Task 3 — The story in sixty seconds
paras: Tell the story of Everett and Lincoln, but start with the point: what does it show about speaking? Then add one fact as the reason, and stop.

final: Is it more important to know your point before you speak, or to be able to find it while you speak?
Everett's audience expected a two-hour oration. How do you decide how long a particular listener will really give you?
Is a speaker who always opens with the answer less interesting than one who builds up to it? When would you choose to build up?
From memory: explain the landing plan in four sentences, using the short answer is, recommend that, what I need and the bottom line.
